claims.text: Nearly equiatomic AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles are theorized to possess enhanced thermal stability.
Heating AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles will cause atomic-scale structural rearrangements.
Heating may modify the nanoparticles' lattice parameters.
Heating may nucleate defects in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
In situ aberration-corrected TEM can directly observe the proposed rearrangements in real time.
A high-temperature heating stage integrated with an aberration-corrected TEM is the proposed intervention.
The proposed observations span room temperature to approximately 800–900 °C or above.
An inert or vacuum atmosphere is needed to avoid oxidation during the proposed observations.
Lattice spacing, defect formation, and phase-boundary evolution can be monitored in real time within the nanoparticles.
Elevated temperature activates thermodynamic effects that drive atomic rearrangements.
Thermal atomic rearrangements lead to transient defects or subtle phase transitions in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
High-resolution in situ imaging can visualize the proposed transient defects or phase transitions.
Observation of lattice changes, defects, or transient phase transformations would confirm that thermodynamic contributions stabilize the nanoparticles at high temperature.
Prior theoretical predictions and ex situ analyses provide only static snapshots and no real-time confirmation of AuCoCuNiPt thermal behavior.
Behavior observed under in situ TEM conditions may not represent bulk material behavior or prolonged exposure in reactive environments.
The transition temperatures and magnitudes of lattice modifications have not been conclusively quantified by prior in situ experiments.
The hypothesis is falsified if no atomic-scale structural changes occur during the prescribed heating experiment or if the changes deviate significantly from the predicted response.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis treats defect creation or transient phase transformation as confirmation of enhanced thermal stability, while treating the absence of structural change as falsification. This makes the operational meaning of stability internally ambiguous, because structural invariance could itself be evidence of thermal stability.
